title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Genesee hits pause on a data center as Michigan communities push for rules on power, water and noise.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Saturday, August 1, and our big story today is Genesee County putting the brakes on a key environmental vote for a proposed data center.
That delay is the latest sign that these projects are hitting real resistance in communities worried about what they mean for daily life.
Exactly. The economic development corporation postponed the environmental clearance vote, so Flint-area residents now have extra weeks to dig into traffic, power needs, and industrial noise.
Why does this matter so much right now? We've seen similar pushes in other places.

Data centers have been landing in Michigan because of available land and power, but the scale is new. A single large facility can pull hundreds of megawatts, which is like adding a small city to the grid.
And that power has to come from somewhere. Does that mean higher bills for everyone nearby?
It can. Utilities often pass along the cost of upgrades, and if the demand spikes fast without new generation, rates can rise for residential customers too.
Water is another big piece, right? Cooling these places takes a lot.
Yes, evaporative cooling can use millions of gallons a day. In places drawing from rivers or aquifers, that raises questions about supply for farms and homes.
And farmland gets turned into industrial sites. How has that played out in other townships?
We've seen several communities hit pause to write new rules. Otsego just voted a full year-long ban on new proposals so they can study noise and grid strain first.
That breathing room seems to be the pattern. What happens next in Genesee?
The extra review period lets the public submit comments on impacts before any final decision. Local officials will have to weigh job promises against those resident concerns.
Who are the main players pushing for or against these projects?
Economic development groups and developers highlight construction jobs and long-term tax revenue. Residents and some local leaders focus on protecting quality of life and infrastructure capacity.
And the noise complaints we've heard elsewhere — like in Dowagiac — are they showing up in Genesee too?
The delay specifically mentions industrial noise as one of the issues residents want more time to review, so yes, it's on the table.
How many other places are in similar holding patterns right now?
At least a handful have enacted temporary bans or required extra studies. It seems like the conversation is shifting from 'yes or no' to 'under what conditions.'
What could tip the scale one way or the other in Genesee?

If the public comments show strong opposition or if power and water studies come back with big red flags, the project could face stricter conditions or rejection. Developers might also scale back plans.
And if it moves forward, what timeline are we talking?
The extra weeks of review push any final vote later into the summer or fall, giving everyone more runway to prepare.
Let's move to quick hits. Yesterday in Saline, Senate candidate El-Sayed rallied at a data center site to criticize tax breaks and grid strain.
He used the project as a backdrop to argue that hyperscale builds are driving up electric rates for residents 30 minutes away.
That stop shows how local projects are now part of the broader primary debate.
Also yesterday, neighbors near the Dowagiac facility described a constant high-pitched whine running day and night.
Those complaints are already influencing how Cass County plans to handle future proposals, with calls for stronger noise protections.
A U.S. representative is asking Commerce to review Chinese robots at the Hyperscale Data Michigan site.
The concern is supply-chain security and whether it affects local construction jobs. It could bring new federal scrutiny.
On Thursday, the Saline data center applied for a river discharge permit, now open for public comment.
Residents in Washtenaw County are watching potential water quality and usage impacts closely.
Also on Thursday, the District C county council race is shaping up around whether to pause AI server farms until power and zoning rules are ready.
Both contenders say the county needs time to study demand before approving more large projects.
Today, Otsego city council voted a one-year halt on all new data center proposals.
That gives residents near potential sites time to help shape rules protecting neighborhoods from noise and grid strain.
Mason County is pitching itself as the home for Michigan's official state data center.
Local leaders see construction jobs and tax revenue, but residents would face questions on power and land use if it advances.
Coldwater is holding a joint meeting today for residents to get their first look at proposed data center plans.
People want details on power and water draw plus any tax breaks on the table, especially with similar fights nearby.
Verrus is pushing ahead on a Michigan project even while its Salem plans remain uncertain.
The company hasn't named the exact site or size, but officials are already fielding questions on power demand and tax deals.
On deck, are there any meetings listeners can attend in the coming days?
Nothing on the calendar yet for the weekend, but we'll keep an eye on Genesee as the public comment window opens and any follow-up sessions get scheduled.
Coldwater's briefing today is one to watch if you're in that area.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Genesee County Delays Data Center Vote, Giving Residents More Time to Weigh Power and Nois
